restatements.text: Titles the measure the Retirement and Personal Savings Protection Act of 2026.
Declares that Californians face high taxes and living costs, and that the measure intends to protect personal savings, pensions, and investments from new and retroactive taxes.
States the purpose is to prohibit new taxes on personal property and retirement holdings, and to require all new taxes to apply prospectively.

Amends the California Constitution to prohibit any state law or future constitutional provision from enacting or authorizing a new tax on the ownership or control of retirement holdings, individually-owned assets, and other personal savings. Exempts taxes in effect and collected on or before December 31, 2025, and does not alter the taxation of real property.

Prohibits the state from imposing new retroactive taxes based on conduct or status occurring before the law's effective date, with an exception for taxes passed by the Legislature that are retroactive for no more than 365 days and whose revenues are strictly dedicated to a declared emergency or fiscal emergency.

Defines protected assets to include pensions, retirement accounts, mutual funds, and all personal property, including financial assets, business interests, digital assets, intellectual property, and personal belongings. Defines 'tax' as any levy imposed by the state under Article XIII A.
Applies the prohibitions to all statewide initiatives submitted to voters on or after January 1, 2026.
Declares that if this measure receives more votes than a conflicting initiative on the same ballot, the conflicting measure shall be null and void.
Provides that if any part of the measure is found invalid, the remaining parts shall remain in effect.
States the measure takes effect at the earliest possible date and becomes operative immediately.
Directs that the measure be liberally construed to achieve its purposes.

Requires the Attorney General to appoint independent counsel to defend the measure if state officials refuse to do so, and establishes a continuous appropriation from the General Fund to cover those legal costs.

evidence.why: It reduces the state's taxing authority by constitutionally prohibiting new taxes on the ownership or control of personal property.

analysis.answer: Current law generally permits the state to enact new forms of taxation, including potential wealth taxes, subject to existing constitutional limitations. This measure amends the state constitution to strictly prohibit any new state tax on the ownership or control of virtually all forms of non-real-estate personal property, including retirement accounts and business interests.

Under current law, the legislature has some discretion to apply tax changes retroactively if doing so meets due process standards. This measure broadly prohibits retroactive taxes based on conduct or status prior to a law's effective date, providing only a narrow exception for a declared emergency with retroactivity limited to 365 days.

The direct cost includes the continuous appropriation from the General Fund to pay for independent counsel if state officials decline to defend the measure. There is also an opportunity cost of foregone state revenue that could otherwise have been raised through taxes on personal property or investments.

Individuals and businesses holding significant non-real-estate assets (such as retirement accounts, stock portfolios, business interests, and intellectual property) benefit by being shielded from potential future wealth or ownership taxes. The cost of future revenue needs will likely be borne by the general public either through increased reliance on other tax bases (such as sales or income taxes) or through reduced public services.

Because personal property and investments are constitutionally shielded from ownership taxes, individuals and businesses may be incentivized to hold wealth in these protected asset classes rather than in forms that remain taxable (such as real property). Lawmakers facing revenue demands will be forced to look to alternative, constitutionally permitted revenue sources.

The measure addresses the perceived threat of future 'wealth taxes' that could erode personal savings and business investments, as well as the uncertainty caused by retroactive taxation. The mechanism is a sweeping constitutional prohibition on state taxes tied to the ownership or control of personal property, combined with a ban on retroactive tax application.
Owners of substantial personal property and investment assets gain protection from taxation. The Legislature and future voters lose the discretionary power to enact these specific forms of taxes.

Whether prohibiting wealth taxes reliably spurs long-term economic investment and job growth is disputed. Some economists argue that wealth taxes discourage investment and prompt capital flight, while others argue that banning such taxes forces reliance on regressive revenue sources without necessarily delivering broad-based economic growth.

Because the measure operates as a broad prohibition on enacting taxes, direct administrative costs are low. However, its expansive definition of protected assets could generate litigation over whether future levies classify as a prohibited 'tax on ownership' versus a permitted tax on transactions or income.
As a constitutional amendment, it can only be undone or modified by another voter-approved amendment to the California Constitution.

flags.quote: “Retirement holdings, individually-owned assets, and other forms of personal savings” means pensions; retirement accounts including but not limited to 401(k) accounts, 403(b) accounts, and all other individual retirement accounts; mutual funds; and all personal property, whether tangible or intangible, including but not limited to financial assets, investment accounts, business interests, digital assets, intellectual property, personal belongings, and other assets used to produce or collect income or savings for retirement or financial planning.
flags.note: The definition of protected assets is highly expansive, sweeping in virtually all forms of non-real-estate tangible and intangible property.

flags.quote: Notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in Chapter 6 (commencing with Section 12500) of Part 2 of Division 3 of Title 2 of the Government Code or any other law, the Attorney General shall appoint independent counsel
flags.note: Uses override language to bypass existing statutes governing the Attorney General's legal duties and discretion.

flags.quote: The provisions of this Act are severable.
This Act shall take effect at the earliest possible date in accordance with Section 10 of Article II of the California Constitution. This Act shall become operative on the same day it takes effect.
flags.note: Specifies that the measure becomes operative immediately upon taking effect.
